pull.title: http: support unix sockets
pull.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/5029

Accept unix socket paths as options for `-rpcbind=` (server) and `-rpcconnect=` (bitcoin-cli). Options follow the same pattern as `ipcbind`:

- `=unix` is a magic keyword that means `<datadir>/http.sock`
- `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path`
- `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path`

We delete any existing `http.sock` before calling `bind()` and do not clean up at shutdown.

Because access is handled by the filesystem, `-rpcallowip` is ignored for unix sockets and not required at all if we are *only* binding to unix sockets.

Authentication by username/password/cookie is still required.

A new option `--httpunix` is added to the test framework and added to test_runner for `rpc_bind.py` and `interface_http.py` for CI, but (like `--usecli`) most other tests should also pass with that option. When set, bitcoind is started with `-rpcbind=unix...`which overrides `tcp://localhost` entirely. `AuthProxy` has been extended to connect directly to the unix socket.

Try it out!
```
bitcoind -regtest -rpcbind=unix
bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix getbestblockhash
```

Refactored code:

Back in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27375 we added unix socket support but it was isloated to the `Proxy` class. That created a bit of tech debt which we pay off in this PR. Two new classes are implemented:
- `UnixSocketAddr` reflects the `CService` API for generic unix sockets, without bitcoin-p2p-specific attributes
- `SocketAddr` holds a variant of `UnixSocketAddr` and `Cservice` so classes like `Proxy` and `HTTPServer` can operate on an abstract level, with either socket type.
- `CNetAddr` and `CService` are left untouched -- they are somewhat dirty combinations of generic socket classes and bitcoin p2p code, adding unix sockets to those classes wouldn't make sense for bitcoin p2p operations and that's why this design was chosen.

Follow-up suggestions:
- Deduplicate some of the unix socket path resolution code between IPC and HTTP
- On macos the default unix socket buffer size is only ~8k. In the functional tests we have to bump the python client socket buffer up to ~256k or the "throttle" tests will stall on macos. We could apply this socket option on the server side as well, only on macos... requires some bike shedding.
- This option replaces TCP but it does not replace HTTP, there may be a more efficient transport protocol.


Production code and test framework changes designed and authored by my own cranial meatball. Unit tests added by Opus. C++ cleaned up by Fable, security tightened by Kimi-k3 🧠 🤖 🤖 🤖

**concept** ACK

---

users of other projects that rely on Core have always wanted sth similar to this and implemented workarounds in the meantime:

- https://github.com/spesmilo/electrum/issues/4955
- https://github.com/btcsuite/btcd/issues/2149

there was also an attempt to add this back in 2017:

- https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/9919

unfortunately, that attempt ran into a limitation in libevent's HTTP client. supporting Unix Domain sockets in `bitcoin-cli` required a libevent patch to pass an already-open Unix socket connection to the HTTP client. this was eventually addressed in https://github.com/libevent/libevent/pull/1722, but by then Core had decided to  moved away from libevent. anyway, with libevent dropped, this is no longer an issue

Don't forget https://github.com/libevent/libevent/issues/1615 ! Its been a long time coming... now that that [pesky little refactor](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35182) is out of the way we can finally get to it ;-)

concept ACK...i found an issue by running two nodes and noticed that second node can take over a live rpc unix socket path,  if two nodes use different datadirs but the same -rpcbind=unix:<path> the second node starts with no error..since it removes the first node socket file and creates its own then after that bitcoin cli talks to the second node.. the first node keeps running but becomes unreachable so with TCP the second bind fails with address already in use

i reproduced this on regtest
```
B=build/bin
SOCK=/tmp/btc-hijack.sock
mkdir -p /tmp/nodeA /tmp/nodeB
ARGS="-regtest -daemon -listen=0 -rpcbind=unix:$SOCK -rpcuser=u -rpcpassword=p"
CLI="$B/bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix:$SOCK -rpcuser=u -rpcpassword=p -rpcwait"
```

1: **for node A**
```
$B/bitcoind -datadir=/tmp/nodeA $ARGS
$CLI getrpcinfo | grep logpath && stat -c 'inode=%i' $SOCK

output:
Bitcoin Core starting
"logpath": "/tmp/nodeA/regtest/debug.log"
inode=2229678
```

2: **for node B**
```
$B/bitcoind -datadir=/tmp/nodeB $ARGS; sleep 2
$CLI getrpcinfo | grep logpath && stat -c 'inode=%i' $SOCK

output:
Bitcoin Core starting                                  (as you can see node B starts without error)
"logpath": "/tmp/nodeB/regtest/debug.log"              (cli now reaches B)
inode=2229647   (and this replaces node A socket file)
```

3: ss -xlp | grep btc-hijack
```
output:
u_str LISTEN ... /tmp/btc-hijack.sock ... pid=1684462  (this is for B)
u_str LISTEN ... /tmp/btc-hijack.sock ... pid=1684363  (here A still listening but unreachable)
```

4: $CLI stop; sleep 2
```
output:
Bitcoin Core stopping                                  (`stop` reached B)
```

5: pgrep -a bitcoind
```
output:
1684363 build/bin/bitcoind -datadir=/tmp/nodeA ...     (A still running)
```

6: $CLI -rpcwait=0 getblockcount
```
output:
error: Error while attempting to communicate with server unix:/tmp/btc-hijack.sock (Could not connect to the server)

Make sure the bitcoind server is running and that you are connecting to the correct unix socket path.
Use "bitcoin-cli -help" for more info.
```

i noticed a change in bitcoin-cli the host header contains the resolved IP instead of the hostname given in `-rpcconnect=localhost` the build from master sends `Host: localhost` but on this PR sends `Host: 127.0.0.1`

i reproduced the result by running this py file on terminal 1
```py
import socket

srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 18555))
srv.listen()
print("listening on 127.0.0.1:18555")
while True:
    conn, _ = srv.accept()
    request = conn.recv(4096).decode(errors="replace")
    for line in request.split("\r\n"):
        if line.lower().startswith("host:"):
            print(line)
    conn.close()
 ```
 
 on terminal 2 i ran this command
 ```
 build-master/bin/bitcoin-cli -rpcconnect=localhost -rpcport=18555 -rpcuser=u -rpcpassword=p -rpcclienttimeout=3 getblockcount
build-pr36434/bin/bitcoin-cli       -rpcconnect=localhost -rpcport=18555 -rpcuser=u -rpcpassword=p -rpcclienttimeout=3 getblockcount
```

 and the output was 
 
 ```
 python3 /tmp/show_host.py 
listening on 127.0.0.1:18555
Host: localhost
Host: 127.0.0.1
```

approach ACK

---
i am convinced by the implementation here. particularly, i like the choice of `std::variant` over polymorphism  for the `SocketAddr` class

after staring at the implementation for a while now, i think the changes are mostly in very good shape, with the introduction of `SocketAddr` being the cornerstone change that everything else seems to spring from. most of my reviews have therefore been nitpicks, since i am convinced by the overall design choices. the security is tight too 🔒 

i have mostly been looking at the implementation C++ code and have not yet had an extensive look at the tests or their infrastructure code, beyond a quick perusal

_one last question_: i saw `UnixSocketAddr::SetSockAddr()` handles empty and abstract namespace addresses, but we do not support binding or connecting to abstract sockets. do you think it is worth supporting them in the future for linux-specific setups ?

---

looks like the PR description is out of sync with the code

> * `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path/http.sock`
> 
> * `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path/http.sock`


it says `=unix:relative/path` resolves to `<datadir>/relative/path/http.sock` and `=unix:/absolute/path` to `/absolute/path/http.sock`, but `ResolveUnixSocketAddr()` uses the given path _as the socket file itself_. so `unix:rpc.sock` turns into `<datadir>/rpc.sock`, and `unix:/tmp/rpc.sock` stays `/tmp/rpc.sock`. only the bare `unix` (or `unix:`) keyword uses the default `http.sock` name

the docs, release notes and `-help` text already match the code, so i think the PR description just needs updating to reflect this, so other reviewers do not get tripped up by the mismatch

---

i also think this PR would be a good candidate for v33. there has been interest in this for a long time, and i think it is worth tracking as an upcoming feature for the release

events.message:
netbase: introduce UnixSocketAddr class

Include unit tests to ensure the API matches CService
netbase: refactor Proxy to use SocketAddr
http: use SocketAddr instead of CService
http: support listening on UNIX domain sockets

http: allow empty -rpcallowip if all bind addresses are unix sockets

Co-authored-by: winterrdog <winterrdog@protonmail.ch>

Enable unix sockets in test_framework: cover interface_http & rpc_bind

Most functional tests will pass with --httpunix, which uses unix
sockets instead of TCP for all RPC commands in the test. For now,
only require interface_http, rpc_bind --httpunix in CI to cover
the specific changes from this branch.
bitcoin-cli: support connecting on UNIX domain sockets
doc: add unix socket options to help and docs

comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -0,0 +1,31 @@
+Updated settings
+----------------
+
+- `-rpcbind` now accepts a unix domain socket on platforms that support unix
+  sockets (not Windows), using the same syntax as `-ipcbind`: `-rpcbind=unix`
+  listens on the default path `<datadir>/http.sock`, and
+  `-rpcbind=unix:<path>` listens on a custom path. Relative paths are
+  interpreted relative to the network data directory. The JSON-RPC and REST
+  interfaces are then served over that socket. When every `-rpcbind` value is
+  a unix socket, the default TCP localhost listeners are not bound and
+  `-rpcallowip` is not required. (#36434)
+
+  Connections over a unix socket bypass `-rpcallowip` entirely, so access to the
+  RPC server is controlled by filesystem permissions on the socket file
+  (restricted to the owner after binding) and the permissions of the directory
+  it is placed in, in addition to the usual RPC authentication. The maximum
+  path length, after resolving a relative path against the data directory, is
+  platform dependent, around 100 bytes. Missing parent directories are created
+  (with default permissions, so place the socket in a suitably restricted directory)
+  and a stale socket file left by a previous run is removed at startup. Startup
+  fails if the path exists and is not a socket.
+  The socket file is not removed on shutdown.
+
+Tools and Utilities
+-------------------
+
+- `bitcoin-cli` can connect to a node over a unix domain socket with
comments.body:
**nit:** sometimes, i see that you use "unix socket", while on other occasions it is "unix _domain_ socket". is that intentional, or should we choose uniformity, pick one option, and then just run with it all throughout ?

"unix socket" seems more common in the docs and in the code comments in this PR's diff, so probably the best candidate to go with.

> (not Windows)

TIL: windows has _basic_ support for unix domain sockets (UDS). 

since Windows 10 version `1803` or later, windows has shipped UDS support but _limited_ to `SOCK_STREAM` sockets only: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/commandline/af_unix-comes-to-windows/

  *
  * @param      name     The string provided by the user representing a local path
  *
- * @returns Whether the string has proper format, length, and points to an existing file path
+ * @returns Whether the string has the "unix:" prefix and a path short enough

  */

-class Proxy
+/**
+ * Whether an option value names a unix domain socket rather than a host[:port].
+ * Purely syntactic: platform support and path length are not checked. Callers
+ * should classify a value with this before attempting to parse it as host:port,
+ * because some unix socket values (e.g. "unix:8080") are also valid host:port.
+ *
+ * @param[in] value          The option value
+ * @param[in] allow_default  Also accept the bare keyword "unix", meaning a default path
+ */
+bool IsUnixSocketValue(std::string_view value, bool allow_default);
+
+/**
+ * A UNIX domain socket address (a local filesystem path), exposing the subset
+ * of the CService API needed to create, bind and connect sockets.
+ *
+ * Like CService, an instance may be invalid: constructing from a string that
+ * is not a valid "unix:" path (see IsUnixSocketPath()) yields an object for
+ * which IsValid() returns false. Callers must check IsValid() before use.
+ */
+class UnixSocketAddr
+{
+public:
+    UnixSocketAddr() = default;
+    /** @param[in] path Full address string including the "unix:" prefix */
+    explicit UnixSocketAddr(std::string path) : m_path(std::move(path)) {}
+
+    [[nodiscard]] bool IsValid() const { return IsUnixSocketPath(m_path); }
+    [[nodiscard]] sa_family_t GetSAFamily() const { return AF_UNIX; }
+    /** The full address string including the "unix:" prefix.
+     *  Unix sockets don't have a port but we like to match the CService API. */
comments.body:
**nit**: could you have _possibly_ meant this instead ?

```suggestion
     *  Unix sockets don't have a port but we'd like to match the CService API. */
```

`char` is signed on some platforms (e.g. x86), so bytes above `0x7f` are interpreted as negative values (they wrap around) and also match `c < 0x20`. this means a utf-8 path like `/tmp/josé.sock` could end up being replaced with `"unix"` in the logs

taking `unsigned char` (*even* `uint8_t` *works OK*) in the lambda fixes this (i also switched to `std::ranges` in case you find that more appealing)

```suggestion
        if (std::ranges::any_of(path, [](unsigned char c) { return c < 0x20 || c == 0x7F; })) {
```

why don't we just put this behind an `#ifdef HAVE_SOCKADDR_UN` guard so we skip this code entirely on platforms that do not support unix sockets ?

sure! we can never get here with a `UnixSocketAddr` on those platforms anyway, since those addresses get rejected much earlier. currently this would be a no-op at runtime, but we could avoid compiling code that can never be used on those platforms. seems like we can just sidestep it altogether :)

`strRPCBind` can show up in the logs if the _optional port is included_ in the bind address (e.g. `127.0.0.1:8332`), leading to logs like this one: `Could not bind RPC on address 127.0.0.1:8332 port 8332: Address lookup failed.`


```suggestion
                LogWarning("Could not bind RPC on address %s port %i: Address lookup failed.", host, port);
```

_optional_ style nit: we could make this a `const` initialised from a ternary expression:

```suggestion
    const int protocol{to.IsUnix() ? 0 : IPPROTO_TCP};
```

**nit**: i think we could `std::move` both the host string & collection of socket addresses into the return `pair` object (trivial copy avoidance)

```suggestion
    return {std::move(host), std::move(ret)};
```

when i went through `GetBindAddresses()` and `UnixSocketAddr::PreparePath()`, i noticed that duplicate unix endpoints can go unnoticed. if two `-rpcbind` values resolve to the same path (e.g. `-rpcbind=unix` and `-rpcbind=unix:http.sock`, or the same value in `bitcoin.conf` and perhaps on the command line), `PreparePath()` (later called in `HTTPServer::BindAndStartListening`) removes the first socket file before the second `bind()`. therefore, both binds succeed without sending a warning

is this intentional, or just not something we need to worry about? in the case of TCP, the second bind just fails with `EADDRINUSE` and gets logged. would we expect the same here, or is silently rebinding just fine ?

+    /** The full address string including the "unix:" prefix.
+     *  Unix sockets don't have a port but we like to match the CService API. */
